candidates.title: Superellipse Function: A Powerful Geometric Tool for the Design and Deformation Modeling of Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators With Flexural Patterns Experiencing Tension Loss
candidates.abstract: In this article, we feature the Superellipse function as a geometric and versatile tool for effective design and modeling of flexural patterns (FPs) in tendon-driven continuum manipulators (TD-CMs) with discontinuous cross section geometries. We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces- caused by partially-constrained tendons- on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed using a Superellipse function. Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator's geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior. Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and Superellipse function, we then introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to facilitate intuitive design of a TD-CM with a generic FP geometry experiencing tendon tension loss. To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features, we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed and fabricated based on a Superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.

candidates.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
candidates.comment: Manuscript submitted to IEEE OJ-ITS and is currently under review

candidates.title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
candidates.abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
candidates.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures

candidates.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
candidates.comment: Project page: https://carlhoi.github.io

candidates.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
candidates.abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.
candidates.comment: 7 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables. Prepared for the 13th RSI International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (ICRoM 2025), Tehran, Iran

candidates.title: SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
candidates.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.

candidates.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
candidates.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
candidates.comment: Under review. Project page: https://grounded-in-contact.github.io/. The second and third authors contributed equally

candidates.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
candidates.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.

candidates.title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
candidates.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
candidates.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)

candidates.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.

candidates.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
candidates.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
candidates.comment: Project page: https://www.taekyung.me/jepa-shield

candidates.title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity
candidates.abstract: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.

candidates.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
candidates.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
candidates.comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/

candidates.title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention
candidates.abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.
candidates.comment: Accepted in EACL 2027

candidates.title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
candidates.abstract: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

candidates.title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
candidates.abstract: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

candidates.title: Single-Coordinate Activation Steering for Controllable Social Stance in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Steering one neuron of a small language model can impose a topic or a quirk without training, yet replications show that many published single-neuron recipes are fragile or nonspecific. This paper asks whether an interpersonal stance can be controlled in this manner. The stance studied is a distant crush, a chatbot character that is guarded, intermittently warm and inconsistent. In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.

candidates.title: LM2 Compiling a Language Model into Another Model Weights
candidates.abstract: Deploying a conversational model and a specialist together could avoid maintaining a separate specialist service. We present LM2, which embeds a trained story generator into a larger conversational model. The larger model handles the conversation and invokes the generator for story requests. We constrain the generator arithmetic during training so its calculations can be compiled directly into added model layers. We compare this approach with QwenPU, which executes the stories260K language model on an embedded processor. LM2 requires one host token per generated character, compared with approximately 25,000 for QwenPU. However, its story generator predicts held out text less well, i.e. 1.145 bits per character versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better. The Qwen3.5, 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and generates the same characters as a standalone integer implementation of the inner model in the tested runs. These results illustrate a tradeoff between host-token cost and text-prediction performance.

candidates.title: Think Before You Forecast: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Time Series Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.

candidates.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
candidates.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.

candidates.title: Learning Acceptable Lotteries via Queries: Minimizing Aggregated Violation Distances
candidates.abstract: When deploying an AI system, a developer can randomize over several candidate versions, sending each request to a version chosen at random, to balance the requirements of multiple stakeholders. We study a setting in which each of $n$ stakeholders reveals only whether a proposed lottery over $m$ candidates is acceptable, and each stakeholder's acceptable lotteries lie on one side of an unknown hyperplane. While previous work sought a lottery that every stakeholder accepts, such a lottery need not exist when, for instance, safety and helpfulness requirements are in conflict. We therefore minimize a power mean of the stakeholders' violations; since binary answers reveal neither the size of a violation nor how to compare violations across stakeholders, we measure each violation by a normalized distance to the stakeholder's acceptance boundary. We characterize exactly when accept/reject answers determine these distances. When they do, $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries suffice to learn them, where $\varepsilon$ is the precision of the utilities, and this bound is tight; when they do not, a natural worst-case approach is optimal up to a constant factor, even compared with methods that make unlimited queries. For limited query budgets, we give a sampling algorithm whose number of queries for a given accuracy does not depend on $n$, and show that a deterministic algorithm cannot guarantee a small loss without querying almost all stakeholders. Synthetic experiments illustrate the resulting tradeoff between querying many stakeholders and learning each of them accurately.
candidates.comment: 37 pages, 5 figures, NeurIPS 2026

candidates.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
candidates.comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?". OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=oIzsAcOuYl

candidates.title: CompareDR: Benchmarking Deep Research Reports from Individual Quality to Comparative Merit
candidates.abstract: Deep research systems can produce reports with different evidence, analyses, and conclusions for the same query. A reader deciding which findings to rely on needs to know how well each report meets the task requirements and which differences matter to the answer. A score for a single report can summarize its quality, but it does not identify which contributions make one report more useful than another. We introduce CompareDR, a benchmark that combines task-specific pointwise audits with guideline-based pairwise comparisons. We use passage-linked report representations to locate relevant differences and selective evidence verification to check claims that could affect the judgment. The benchmark comprises 40 Chinese and English tasks from three existing benchmarks, 360 reports from nine systems, 1,099 human-reviewed evaluation criteria, and human preferences elicited through blinded comparisons of 80 report pairs. The hybrid evaluator matches 69 of these 80 preferences (86.25%, Cohen's $κ=0.746$). The benchmark supports both comparisons of research systems and examination of the evidence and analyses behind those judgments.

candidates.title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
candidates.abstract: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.

candidates.title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
candidates.abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.
candidates.comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. 10 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables

candidates.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
candidates.comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables

candidates.title: Feedback Completion Certificates for Repeated Dwell Tasks with Time Windows
candidates.abstract: An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances. For a common spatial predicate and dwell length, removing redundant windows orders the remaining obligations by both endpoints. On every history without an expired obligation, the served windows form a suffix. One boundary and one capped run length therefore preserve the future satisfaction of the original task. On a verified library of branching motion primitives we use this state to recover a feedback policy. For one task type a scalar threshold per run length suffices, with work linear in the number of listed branches per time layer for fixed dwell. Multiple types require a joint recursion. On a quadrotor inspection library the threshold sweep reduced the cost of constructing a reusable full-domain policy, while a sparse Boolean baseline answered a single initial query faster. In a two-station MuJoCo patrol, three task-aware filters all met every window in twelve paired runs each. Of eight initially certified runs, the completion filter retained the certificate in all eight, compared with three for safety-only filtering.
candidates.comment: 37 pages, including appendices with full proofs and experimental details

candidates.title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
candidates.abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

candidates.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
candidates.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
candidates.comment: NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 32 pages, 13 figures. Code and run records: https://github.com/kevinxqiu/reset-dependence

candidates.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
candidates.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

candidates.title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
candidates.abstract: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.
candidates.comment: Accepted into IEEE Access

candidates.title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
candidates.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
candidates.comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to and under review in "International Journal of Intelligent Systems" of Wiley

candidates.title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
candidates.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
candidates.comment: Project page: https://embodiedcity.github.io/MAWAM/

candidates.title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
candidates.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.
candidates.comment: Includes supplementary material

candidates.title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
candidates.abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

candidates.title: Meddies-PII: A Multilingual Framework for Personally Identifiable Information Extraction in Clinical De-identification
candidates.abstract: Multilingual PII extraction in clinical text is limited by scarce governed data and by synthetic corpora whose construction is thinly documented. We present a large multilingual dataset covering seventeen languages, including seven Southeast Asian languages, and nine PII labels. We also document a detailed generation pipeline and release the complete prompts, catalogues, checks and label maps. A compact 350M-parameter BIOES token classifier trained on the resource achieves the highest score on all fifteen public benchmarks, significantly ahead of the strongest of four public systems on fourteen of them, with a mean exact-match F1 of 0.827 against 0.672 for the strongest system. We also tested it, without adaptation, on multilingual benchmarks, including two human-annotated German and Spanish clinical-style corpora, where it is competitive with the best public systems once annotation conventions are aligned, and is best in four of ten MultiGraSCCo languages; the results show that performance transfers across public benchmarks. We also analyse the data and find almost no near-duplicates and no text overlap between training and any evaluation set. The dataset, benchmark, model, generation framework and evaluation code are planned for public release upon acceptance.

candidates.title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
candidates.abstract: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $ν\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. Every atom--sector pair has an initialization-dependent activation clock, representing the time at which the atom would grow to macroscopic size in that sector if the pair evolved in isolation. Processing these clocks in increasing order and selecting a pair whenever neither its atom nor its sector has been selected before determines the sequence of actual learning events. We prove that the GF trajectory converges to the corresponding staircase of learned target components. The task of learning modular addition by a CP model with complex weights falls exactly into this framework after Fourier diagonalization. Its activation clocks are independent and identically distributed, allowing us to combine the GF reduction with known random matching asymptotics and derive an explicit, distribution-free large-system loss curve after time reparametrization. We also obtain an asymptotic formula relating this curve to the original GF training time. For models with real weights, conjugate Fourier modes instead form two-dimensional blocks with richer internal structure. We characterize their rank and border-rank cascade and conjecture that the corresponding GF dynamics follows interleaved multi-stage learning processes.

candidates.title: Representation Alignment Is Only as Good as the Teacher's Behavioral Structure
candidates.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $π_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $π_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
candidates.comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables, including supplementary material

candidates.title: OnCache: Learning Dynamic Caching Schedules for Efficient Diffusion Inference
candidates.abstract: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.

candidates.title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
candidates.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.

candidates.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
candidates.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 41 pages, 6 figures. Project website: https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/

candidates.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
candidates.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures

candidates.title: PAWP-TTS: Phoneme-Aware Weight Programming for Compact Bilingual English-Nepali Speech Synthesis
candidates.abstract: This paper presents PAWP-TTS, a compact non-autoregressive text-to-speech system for English, Nepali, and English-Nepali code-mixed speech at 24 kHz, with no language model at inference. Deterministic pronunciation knowledge lives in a rule- and lexicon-based bilingual frontend that preserves native Nepali contrasts and avoids Hindi phonology, so the network only models acoustics. Counting every learned inference tensor, including the waveform decoder, PAWP-1.5M (1,490,390 parameters, 5.98 MB) reaches 1.50% English and 1.75% Nepali character error rate under a single ASR recognizer, and 5.04% / 4.02% Nepali / English phoneme error rate (PER) on 600 untouched test utterances. Decoder-centric 281K-parameter models (1.1 MB) stay intelligible across three independent seeds, with equal-budget dense models (5.53 +/- 0.08% NE, 5.34 +/- 0.28% EN PER) outperforming K=2 cross-layer shared-basis models (6.35 +/- 0.11% NE, 6.57 +/- 0.47% EN PER). Fixing a frontend/label version mismatch nearly halved Nepali PER, more than any architectural or weight-level change. The paper then studies weight-space programming: inspection-guided, zero-training weight edits. Under strict controls (validation-only selection, one-shot test, paired bootstrap, matched random and same-parameter gradient baselines), edits show real selectivity (27:1 on word-boundary pauses with 96 weights; zero cross-lingual collateral inside language-gated residuals) but no accuracy gain beyond controls. Two apparent targets proved to be label or phonology artifacts. Code, ONNX graphs, and CC BY 4.0 weights are released.
candidates.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Code: https://github.com/Firojpaudel/PAWP_TTS | Audio Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/Firoj112/pawp-tts-demo | Models: https://huggingface.co/Firoj112/pawp-tts-1.5m and https://huggingface.co/Firoj112/pawp-tts-300k

candidates.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
candidates.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
candidates.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Under review at IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)

candidates.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
candidates.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
candidates.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 15 tables

candidates.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
candidates.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.
candidates.comment: 36 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Harness, protocol texts, and pre-registration: https://github.com/fahrellgiovanny/conversation-history-integrity

candidates.title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
candidates.abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

candidates.title: Optimal Bandits with Switching Costs: $(T/\log(T))^{2/3}$ Regret
candidates.abstract: We study adversarial bandits with switching costs. For $K$ arms, $T$ rounds, unit switching costs, and oblivious losses in $[0,1]$, we prove that the minimax regret is \begin{equation*} Θ\!\left(\min\left\{T, \frac{K^{1/3}T^{2/3}}{\log^{2/3}(2+T/K)}\right\}\right)\,. \end{equation*} This shows that simple blocking, which plays one arm throughout each block, is suboptimal. Our algorithm makes at most a constant number of switches at random times within each block. The key idea for the improvement is to extract more information per switch by giving greater weight to observations near switching times. We also introduce detours, during which the learner temporarily plays a newly sampled arm. Larger observed losses make a detour more likely. These detours cancel temporal correlation terms induced by blocking while preserving the observations used in the estimates. A matching lower bound follows from a refined analysis of a modified multiscale random walk construction.
candidates.comment: 22 pages

candidates.title: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
candidates.abstract: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.
candidates.comment: 28 pages, 19 figures, 9 tables

candidates.title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control
candidates.abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing.
